title: On‑Prem KMS & HSM hardening playbook — terraform notes & upgrade plan
body:
Purpose:

This is a working playbook for integrating customer on-prem/private deployments with KMS/HSM-backed key management, improving secrets handling, enabling strong at-rest and in-transit encryption, and tightening audit logging. This doc combines architecture notes, Terraform module guidance, and a pragmatic upgrade and rollback plan. It's intended for eng-private-deployments, platform security, and SREs doing customer rollouts.

Scope:
- Private deployments: VPC and on-prem packages (air-gapped or partially connected)
- Cloud-agnostic KMS patterns: support for AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault, and customer HSM (PKCS#11) integrations
- Terraform modules used by our private control plane and agent installers
- Upgrade plan for moving existing private installs to KMS-backed secrets (non-disruptive)

Assumptions:
- Customer provides network connectivity or a secure bastion for bootstrap (if required)
- For HSM cases, customer can provide PKCS#11 endpoint or Cloud HSM managed cluster
- We maintain a secrets abstraction in the control plane that supports multiple backends (vault, cloud-kms, hsm)

High-level architecture notes:
- Key hierarchy:
  - Root wrapping key: customer-managed HSM/KMS key (never exported).
  - Envelope keys: short-lived data encryption keys (DEKs) generated by our services, encrypted with wrapping key.
  - Token encryption keys: for service tokens, rotated more frequently.

- Recommended flows:
  - On secrets write: service generates DEK -> encrypt data with DEK -> encrypt DEK with KMS/HSM wrapping key -> store ciphertext + encrypted DEK
  - On read: fetch ciphertext + encrypted DEK -> call KMS/HSM decrypt to unwrap DEK (or perform cryptographic operation in-HSM via AEAD) -> decrypt payload

- HSM vs cloud KMS trade-offs:
  - HSM (PKCS#11) gives strict key export controls and FIPS level assurances, but requires driver/connector maintenance.
  - Cloud KMS is easier for hosted environments, provides integrated audit logs and IAM, and can be used over private connectivity for VPC customers.

Terraform module notes (working):
- Module: redwood_kms_connector
  - Inputs (recommended):
    - provider (string): "aws" | "gcp" | "azure" | "hsm"
    - kms_key_id (string): ARN / resource id when provider != hsm
    - hsm_endpoint (string): PKCS11 URI for hsm provider
    - hsm_module_path (string): path on host to PKCS#11 library (for installer templates)
    - key_policy (string): JSON policy template for cloud keys
    - grant_principals (list): list of principal ARNs/ids allowed to use key
    - audit_log_sink (string): logging destination (splunk/datadog/cloud)
  - Outputs:
    - kms_key_resource_id
    - kms_key_policy
    - hsm_connector_config (ca certs, endpoints)  

- Implementation notes:
  - Keep actual secrets out of TF state: module should accept references (e.g., data sources) and avoid storing unencrypted private keys in state. Where unavoidable, use remote state encryption and short TTL state credentials.
  - For HSM, Terraform can't drive HSM key creation in all vendors; prefer a step where operator registers pre-created HSM key with a resource (data source) rather than creating it in code.
  - Provide a 'dry_run' flag that populates expected resources without committing changes (useful for review and codegen of policies).

Example Terraform snippet (illustrative, not copy-paste):

resource "redwood_kms_connector" "customer_primary" {
  provider = "hsm"
  hsm_endpoint = var.hsm_endpoint
  hsm_module_path = var.hsm_module_path
  grant_principals = ["arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/redwood-agent"]
  audit_log_sink = var.audit_sink
}

Security hardening specifics:
- Audit logging:
  - Log every E2E KMS/HSM operation (encrypt/decrypt/sign) with requestor principal, resource id, timestamp, and a correlation id.
  - Forward HSM device logs to a collector running in an isolated namespace; sign and timestamp logs if supported.
  - Keep a separate, immutable write-once storage for key-event logs when customer requires tamper-evidence.
  - Retention: default 90 days for operational teams, archive monthly 7-year cold storage for compliance customers.
  - Suggested fields: {timestamp, request_id, actor, operation, key_id, source_ip, container_id, app_name, correlation_id, result_code}

- Secrets handling patterns:
  - Use envelope encryption; never store plaintext secrets in DB or TF state.
  - Bootstrapping: use an operator-only manual step to register root wrapping key; operator can supply a KMS key ARN or HSM slot id.
  - Auto-unseal for Vault: recommend using HSM/KMS for Vault auto-unseal; for air-gapped, use offline sealed key with rotation policy.
  - Short-lived secrets: service tokens should be minted with TTL <= 1hr and refreshed via a token service that has restricted scope and auditable issuance.

- Key rotation and rewrap:
  - Rotating wrapping keys should trigger an asynchronous rewrap job that iterates DEKs and re-encrypts them with the new key; do not block reads while rewrap in progress.
  - Maintain backward compatibility: allow previous key versions to remain readable until all rewrap jobs complete.
  - Plan for staged rotation: canary subset -> bulk -> verify checksums

- Network and transport hardening:
  - Enforce mTLS for control-plane <-> agents communications for all private deployments.
  - Require TLS 1.3, disable legacy ciphers. Mutual TLS certs can be stored in Vault and provisioned via agent bootstrap.
  - For HSM connectivity, prefer private routes (VPC peering / AWS PrivateLink / GCP VPC-SC) over public endpoints.

Upgrade plan (non-disruptive migration to KMS-backed secrets):
- Goals: no downtime for customer workloads, minimal operator manual steps, clear rollback.

Pre-upgrade (planning):
- Inventory: run a job to list all existing secrets, their current encryption status, and owners. Output CSV to /tmp/upgrade-inventory-<date>.csv
- Tests: create a staging deployment that mirrors production with a subset of secrets and sample HSM/KMS backend.
- Backups: snapshot existing DB, secret-store backups, and agent configurations.

Canary phase:
1. Deploy redwood-agent vX.Y with KMS-capable secret fetch code to 5% of nodes (canary tag). Agents still accept legacy secrets and new KMS-wrapped secrets.
2. Register wrapping key (operator step) to the control plane for canary. Validate decrypt ability via smoke test (INFRA-4123).
3. Rewrap 1% of non-critical secrets and verify read/write by canary agents.
4. Monitor audit logs and latency impact for 72 hours. Check error rates and KMS call budget.

Bulk migration:
- Progressive batches (10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with verification windows between each.
- Rewrap job workers operate in low-priority pool; throttle to ensure latency SLOs unaffected.
- Final sweep ensures no legacy unwrapped secrets remain unless explicitly opted out.

Rollback:
- If canary shows failures (error rate > 0.5% or latency P95 regression > 30%), stop rewraps and revert agents to previous config (feature-flag off) and use backups to restore any partially migrated secret states.
- Log the failure with correlation_id and create postmortem ticket.

Operational runbook (short checklist):
- Before:
  - Create Jira ticket referencing INFRA-4123
  - Confirm backup snapshots exist and are validated
  - Notify customer and schedule maintenance window (if customer policy requires)
- During:
  - Enable canary flag for agents
  - Register wrapping key and run smoke tests
  - Start rewrap worker with throttle 5 ops/sec
  - Watch audit log streams (search: "kms_decrypt failures" and "wrap_errors")
- After:
  - Increase rollout percentages per schedule
  - Validate token-rotation approvals and re-issue service tokens
  - Archive migration logs and mark ticket with run_id

Open questions / TODOs:
- HSM vendor support matrix: need exact PKCS#11 quirks for Thales, Utimaco, and AWS CloudHSM (create INFRA-4241).
- Terraform remote state: how to avoid leaking HSM module path in state for air-gapped installers? (proposal: render installer templates with placeholders and inject at runtime.)
- Cost model: estimate extra KMS calls per 1M secrets reads and customer bill impact.
- Decide default audit retention per compliance tier (GDPR vs SOC2 vs FedRAMP customers).

References and artifacts:
- Jira: INFRA-4123 (KMS integration spike), INFRA-4241 (HSM vendor matrix)
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules#98 (work-in-progress for redwood_kms_connector)
- Confluence: Private Deployments > Security Hardening (draft)
